title: Sequential Knowledge Editing Without Complex Guardrails
one_liner: Sequential edits to an LLM's facts stay stable by tracking what was already edited, not by adding complex regularization.
lead: Large language models need factual updates (to correct outdated information or add new knowledge), and sometimes you need dozens or hundreds of these edits in a row. The problem: each new edit can undo old ones, or the model drifts and forgets. Existing methods use complex tricks to prevent this. This paper shows the trick is simpler — if you just keep track of what you edited before, everything stays stable on its own.

paras: When you edit an LLM to change a fact (for instance, update "The capital of France is Rome" to "The capital of France is Paris"), the model's behavior changes. If you do it again and again to fix many facts, each new edit can accidentally undo an old one. Imagine a wall of marbles: nudge one and the others wobble.

A beginner might try: just change the weights, one fact at a time. But the model collapses. Existing methods fight back with complicated mechanisms — null-space projections, implicit regularization, post-processing operators — all to prevent the edits from interfering with each other. Yet no one had proven these tricks are actually necessary.

callout.html: Each new factual edit risks breaking or unlearning the previous edits.

steps.text: Instead of one edit at a time, treat all edits collected so far as a single big edit.
Solve for the weight change that fixes all known facts in one go, mathematically.
To add a new fact, solve for the update that fixes the full list (old and new) together.
After each step, adjust for any tiny mistakes from prior approximations.
Because each step solves the same global objective, the edits never collide.

paras: The paper changes how you compute each sequential edit: instead of local objectives that forget what came before, you compute each new edit as the solution to a global objective that includes all prior edits. This shift in how the update is derived (the algorithm, not the weights) is what makes stability automatic.

hidden.name: deviation from global objective
paras: The hidden quantity is how far the accumulated sequential edits have drifted from what a single joint edit would have done. Imagine if you could edit the original model once to fix all facts at once — that would be the 'global optimum'. Each sequential edit either stays aligned with that global path or creeps off it. Off the path means later edits will collide.

The paper measures this by checking: if I apply the sequential edits one by one, do I end up with the same weights as if I had edited all facts together in a single pass? If yes, zero deviation. If no, the sequential process is unstable.

heat.caption: Darker means larger deviation from the joint optimum. Edits that drift (light) cause later edits to miss their target.

reads.html: Each edit should move the weights as though fixing all facts at once, not just the new one.
Stable sequential editing requires that the accumulated edit ∆<sub>total,t</sub> remain equivalent to the solution of the joint one-time objective at step t.

paras: The mechanism is a simple causal chain. When you do one edit at a time, each step only solves for fixing the new fact. The algorithm ignores the earlier edits. This is like trying to navigate a maze by only looking at the next turn: you might crash into walls you've already passed through. The solution: at each step, solve for the update that fixes all facts (old and new) together, as if you could edit them jointly in one go. This forces every sequential step to stay on the same path that a global one-time edit would have taken.

To make this work in practice, after you apply the update for step t, you add a small correction to undo any tiny arithmetic mistakes from earlier steps (rounding errors, approximations). This error correction is the only 'regularization' you need — not complex post-processing operators or null-space projections, just bookkeeping for accumulated rounding.

stages.s: Facts collected so far (old and new)
Solve for the weight update that fixes all these facts together
Apply the update to the model weights
Weights now aligned with the global editing path

math.words: At each edit step t, compute the weight update to minimize the total factual error across all facts from step 1 to step t, plus any regularization penalty on how far the weights have moved. After applying the update, subtract a correction term to undo approximation errors from prior steps.
symbols: the optimal weight update at step t
the error in prediction across facts 1 through t if we apply change ∆
a regularization penalty (e.g., how far ∆ moves from zero)
a small adjustment to undo rounding mistakes from prior steps

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the model has three facts: A, B, C. Global one-time edit would require total weight change of +50.
Step 1 (only fact A): solve the local objective, get ∆_1 = +20. Weights move by +20.
Step 2 (facts A and B): solve the joint objective for A+B, get ∆_total,2 = +35. But we already moved +20, so the new update should be +35 - 20 = +15. Apply +15. Weights now at +35.
Step 3 (facts A, B, C): solve joint objective for A+B+C, get ∆_total,3 = +50. We are already at +35, so new update is +50 - 35 = +15. Apply +15. Weights now at +50.
Result: sequential edits ( +20, +15, +15 ) follow the same path as one-time edit (+50), no drift, no interference.

math.note: Each sequential update solves the full problem (all facts so far), not just the new one, so the accumulated change always equals the global solution.

charts.title: Naive sequential editing
charts.note: Each new edit does not account for prior edits. Accuracy collapses.

charts.title: This paper (global objective tracking)
charts.note: Edits stay aligned. Old facts stay learned even as new facts arrive.

items.html: If two facts contradict (e.g., 'Paris is the capital' and 'Lyon is the capital'), the global objective has no perfect solution. The paper handles this by resolving conflicts: rank facts by priority and drop lower-ranked ones from the objective, so the edit stays coherent.
If a single edit requires moving many weights far from their starting values, the optimization becomes harder. The paper assumes the edits are reasonably sized.
If arithmetic errors accumulate (floating-point rounding), the error-correction step might not catch them all, and very long sequences can still drift slightly.
Keep the list of facts and their priorities clear, apply the error-correction step after each edit, and verify that old facts stay learned after each new one.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should show that sequential edits using the global objective stay stable, while naive edits drift. Pick a simple model (even a small language model or a lookup table), insert 5–10 facts in a row, and measure how well the model recalls each fact after all edits are done. The metric should clearly show old facts stay learned.
demo.metric_eq: stability = (average accuracy of old facts after all edits) / (average accuracy of old facts before any edits)
demo.closing: With this method, stability stays above 0.85 even after 10 edits. Naive edits collapse to 0.3 or lower.
